Death of fish in Yamuna 
* 82. SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the newspaper report 
titled "Pollution authorities worry as fish die in Yamuna", which appeared in 
the Asian Age, New Delhi on 21st June, 2002; and 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken to save aquatic life and increase 
the efficiency of sewage treatment plants in the river stretch of 
Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government is aware of the incident of death of 
fishes in River Yamuna on 13th and 17th June, 2002 in the stretch from Agra to 
Bateshwar. The Central Pollution Control Board carried out detailed survey and 
water quality monitoring along this stretch.The findings of Central Pollution 
Control Board revealed that low flow in the river necessitated release of water 
in a regulated manner from Gokul Barrage. But instead there was a sudden release 
of water which may have resulted in scouring of organic matter in the river bed. 
High quantity of churned organic matter in the river water might have lead to 
depletion of oxygen and resulting in fish mortality. 
1

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
The steps taken by the Government to save aquatic life and to increase 
the efficiency of the sewage treatment plants in the river stretch of Delhi are as 
under:— 
(i) Directions under Section 18(1)(b) of the Water Act, 1974 have been 
issued by the Central Pollution Control Board to the concerned State Boards along 
the River Yamuna including the State of Delhi for taking steps to properly 
operate and maintain the sewage treatment plants, provide facilities for collection 
and treatment of sewage, to comply with the effluent standards strigently for 
industries located along river Yamuna and to maintain basic minimum flow 
for protection of the aquatic life besides other directions. 
(ii) Under Yamuna Action Plan Phase-I, pollution abatement schemes have 
been undertaken in 8 towns of Uttar Pradesh and 12 towns of Haryana besides Delhi. 
The physical progress of the works is 95 per cent. 
(iii) The Delhi Government has taken the following measures:— 
(a) Improvement of the capacity utilization of sewage treatment plants 
by desilting and rehabilitation of trunk sewer. 
(b) Upgrading the existing capacity of sewage treatment plants by 
improving the various parameters of pollution. 
(c) The performance of sewage treatment plants in minitored on 
quarterly basis. 
(d) The effluent standards for sewage treatment plants has been made 
more stringent with respect to Biochemicals Oxygen Demand (10 
miligrams per litre as against 30 miligrames per litre) and Total 
Suspended solids (15 miligrams per litre as against 50 miligrams 
per litre). 
(e) Organising training courses by Delhi Productivity Council for the 
staff engaged for operation and maintenance of sewage treatment 
plants. 
(iv) A High Powered Committee has been constituted under the 
chairmanship of Member (Environment), Planning Commission with Chief 
Secretaries of Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh 
as members, to discuss various issues for maintaining the minimum flow in 
river Yamuna. 
2 

[19 July, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(v) A Water Quality Assesment Authority and State Level Review 
Committees have been constituted to ensure the maintenance of water quality 
of surface and ground waters.

Statement 
NCERT is an autonomous body of the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development. It is registered under the Societies Registration Act (Act XXI of 
1860). The objects of  the Council, as enumerat ed in the Memorandum of 
Association (MoA) are to assist and advise the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development in the implementation of its policies and major programmes in 
the field of education, particularly school education. The MoA also stipulates 
that for realization of these objectives, the Council may, amongst other 
programmes and activities, advise the State Governments and other educational 
organizations and institutions on matters relating to school education. Annual 
Accounts of the NCERT are audited by the C & AG. Annual Accounts, Audit 
Report and Annual Report, after they are approved by the General Body of the 
council, are laid on the Tables of both the Houses of Parliament by Central 
Government.

confidence' in the NCERT in the recent meeting of its General Body. The various 
activities and programme of the NCERT were discussed and State representatives

proposal under consideration to make any changes in the functioning of the 
NCERT.

* 92. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state:

the bird catchers in India are still trading in many endangered birds and 
poaching the endangered animals; 
(b) if so, the details of such activities detected during the last three years;

practices? 
37 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Trade in rare and endangered species of birds is prohibited. 
However, incidences of illegal trade of birds are detected from time to time 
and are dealt with as per the provision of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. 
(b)The enforcement of Wild life (Protection) Act, 1972 is mainly done 
by the State Governments. The statistics about seizure made by the State 
Governments officials are not complied and collated by the Central 
Government. However, the details of seizures made by the Regional Dy. Directors, 
Wild Life Preservation, Ministry of Environment and Forests, for the last three 
years are given in the Statement {See below). 
(c)The steps taken by Government to stop illegal bird trade are as 
follows: 
(1) Steps taken at the State Level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting and 
commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have been set up 
in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(iii) State Wildlife Authorities carry out regular checking of the stocks of 
dealers in birds. 
(2) Steps taken at National Lavel: 
(i) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Offices for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country 
to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife 
offenders. Anti poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(iii) Export of wild animals and th eir derivatives is prohibited under 
EXIM policy.

(i) Government of India seeks international co-operation under the 
provisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered 
Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade 
in wildlife items.

Impact of pollution on heart disease 
331. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will 
the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a new study has pointed out that air pollution has a 
significant impact on heart diseases; 
(b) if so, whether according to the st udy, early 40,000 people die of air 
pollution every year in Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Kanpur and 
Nagpur; 
(c) whether the study found a rise in coronary events within 24 to 48 hours 
after pollution increase in Delhi; and 
(d) if so, what steps are being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) The study entitled "Outdoor Air Pollution and Emergency Room 
Visits at a Hospital in Delhi" carried out by the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS), New De lhi, indicates manifestations of respiratory and 
cardio-vascular diseases attributable to air pollution. Degree of relationship 
amongst levels of pollutants, temperature, humidity etc. was assessed by using 
statistical models. A time lag of 24 hours improved the correlation between the 
levels of pollutants and the observe events. However, according to the authors, 
the study had limitations in the assessment of both exposure and outcome 
variables and as such the findings of the present study should be taken as 
preliminary observations. Further, the AIIMS Study did not investigates mortality 
due to air pollution. 
(d-) The steps taken by the Government to control air pollution include the 
following: 
(i)  A comprehensive Policy for Abatement of Pollution which lays stress 
on the preventive and control aspects of pollution has been evolved. 
(ii) Emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission standards 
for new vehicles have been notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, 
1988 and are enforced by the various Transport Departments of the 
State Governments including Delhi. 
81 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
(iii) Unleaded petrol is supplied in the entire country from 1.2.2000 and 
diesel with 0.25% sulphur maximum content is supplied from 1.1.2000 
in the entire country. Ultra low sulphur (0.05%) fuel has also been 
introduced in major cities. 
(iv) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is supplied to automobiles through a 
number of retail outlets in Delhi and Mumbai to cater to the CNG 
vehicles. 
(v) Benzene content in petrol has been reduced. 
(vi) A network of 295 Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations has been 
set up throughout the country. 
(vii) Emission standards for industries have been notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
(viii) Steps have been taken to control pollution from 17 categories of highly 
polluting industries. 
(ix) Industries are also required to provide necessary pollution control 
measures before commissioning of their plants. 
(x) Industries are require to take consent from the respective State 
Pollution Control Board under the Water (Prevention and Control of 
Pollution) Act, 1974, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 
1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for discharging 
their effluent and hazardous waste. 
(xi) Environmental Action Plans for 24 critically polluted areas have been 
prepared and are under implementation.

Air pollution in major cities 
336. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Air pollution goes to the heart", as reported in the Times of India', 
dated the 17th June, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether, according to th e World Bank Study, nearly forty 
thousand people die every year in India in some big cities only, due to air 
pollution; 
(c) if so, whether the CPCB has since undertaken any concrete plans to 
check air pollution in major cities of the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. However, there is no conclusive data available to 
confirm mortality attributable to air pollution. 
(c) and (d) The major steps taken by the Government as well as CPCB 
to control air pollution are mentioned below: 
(i) A comprehensive Policy for Abatement of Pollution which lays stress 
on the preventive and control aspects of pollution has been evolved. 
(ii) Emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission 
standards for new vehicles have been notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, 
1988 and are enforced by the various Transport Departments of the State 
Governments including Delhi. 
(iii) Unleaded petrol is supplied in the entire country from 1.2.2000 and 
diesel with 0.25% sulphur maximum content is supplied from 1.1.2000 in the entire 
country. Ultra low sulphur (0.05%) fuel has also been introduced in major cities. 
(iv) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is supplied to automobiles through 
a number of retail outlets in Delhi and Mumbai to cater to the CNG vehicles. 
(v) Benzene content in petrol has been reduced. 
89 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
(vi) A network of 295 Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations has 
been set up throughout the country. 
(vii) Emission standards for industries have been notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
(viii) Steps have been taken to control pollution from 17 categories of 
highly polluting industries. 
(ix) Industries are also required to provide necessary pollution control 
measures before commissioning of their plants. 
(x) Industries are required to take consent from the respective State Pollution 
Control Board under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the 
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986 for discharging their effluent and hazardous waste. 
(xi) Environmental Action Plans for 24 critically polluted areas have been 
prepared and taken up for implementation.

Death of fishes in Yamuna in Agra 
348. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR RE DDY: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some time back, thousands of fish were found 
dead in a short of stretch of the Yamuna river in Agra; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any inquiry has been made to find out the reasons for this 
incident; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) the steps taken to ensure that untreated sewage and industrial 
effluents are not dumped indiscriminately into the river by the industries? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) the incident of fish mortality in river Yamuna were reported 
on 13th and 17th June, 2002 in the stretch from Agra to Bateshwar. The Central 
Pollution Control Board (CPCB) carried out detailed survey 
105 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
and water quality monitoring in this stretch.The findings of CPCB revealed 
that low flow in the river and sudden release of water from Gokul Barrage, 
might have resulted in scouring of organic matter in the river bed and that 
high quantity of organic matter might have lead to depletion of oxygen in the 
river water causing fish mortality. 
(e)The CPCB has issued directions under Section 18(1)(b) of the Water 
Act, 1974, to Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board, Haryana State Pollution 
Control Board and Delhi Pollution Control Committee for taking steps to 
properly operate and maintain the sewa ge treatment plants, provide facilities 
for collection and treatment of sewage in the State and to comply with the 
effluent standards stgringently for industries located along river Yamuna. 
PM's Intervention in imports of genetically modified foods 
349. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry of Agriculture has sought Prime Minister's 
intervention to make imports of genetically modified foods transparent; 
(b) if so, whether in the absence of  an appropriate frame-work, GM 
foods were entering the country; 
(c) whether there have been reports that India was importing huge 
quantities of Soya oils, extracted from GM seeds; 
(d) whether the Ministry of Agriculture had also written to his Ministry 
to issue necessary notifi cation under the Environment Protection Act, 1986; 
and 
(e) if so, what has been the Prime Minister's response on this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) It is not correct to say that there is no appropriate 
framework for import of GM foods in the country. Rule 11 of the 
Manufacture, use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous 
Microorganisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989 notified 
under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, provides that foods stuffs, 
ingredients in food stuffs 
106 

[19 July, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
and additives including processing aids containing or consisting of 
genetically engineered organisms or cells, shall not be produced, sold, 
imported or used except with the ap proval of the Genetic Engineering 
Approval Committee (GEAC). Thus, import of genetically modified food 
requires the approval of GEAC. There is no such information available in 
this Ministry that huge quantities of soya oil extracted from GM seeds is 
imported in the country. 
(d)The Ministry of Agriculture requested the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests to issue a notification und er the Environment (Protection) Act 
making it binding on importers to declare whether the commodity being 
imported is of GM or non-GM origin, and in case of GM to obtain a 
necessary permit from the Ministry of Environment and Forests for its 
import. 
(e) The Prime Minister's office convened an interministerial meeting to 
discuss issues in biotechnology regulation. The meeting decided that a small 
group be set up to review the existing structure of biotechnology regulation 
and suggest measures for changes, if required.

24 Finance Ministers, including India, approved the proposal; and

primary education by 2015 and eliminate gender disparities in education 
by 2005, to meet the Millenium Development Goal on gender equality in 
Primary and Secondary Education. The Action Plan decided in the meeting includes 
strengthening information systems and data based to ensure outcome focussed

Governent of India has introduced the Constitution (93rd Amendment) Bill in 
Parliament to make elementary education a Fundamental Right for all 
children in the age-group 6-14 years. It has also  launched the natioal

366.   DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR.AKHILESHDAS: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the orders issued 
by the Supreme Court directing the Central and State Governments to provide 
cooked mid-day meals in all the schools, from January, 2002, stressing that this 
implement the Constitution (93rd Amendment) Bill, 2001, and would provide 
a major boost for below poverty line families to educate their children; 
(b) if so, what steps have since been taken by the Central and the State 
Governments to ensure provision of cooked mid-day meals to school children, 
indicating the provision of funds for the schemes; and 
(c) how far this has given a boost to school enrolments? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) The 
Hon'ble Supreme Court vide their order dated 28.11.2001 have directed 
126 

[19 July, 2002] RAJYA    SABHA 
States/UTs to implement the Mid-day Meal Scheme by providing every child 
in every Government and Government assisted primary schools with a 
prepared mid-day meal with a minimum content of 300 calories and 8-12 
grams of protien each day of school  for a minimum of 200 days. Those 
Governments providing dry rations instead of cooked meals must within 
three months start providing cooked meals in all Government and 
Government aided primary schools in all half the districts of the State (in 
order of poverty) and must within a further period of three months extend the 
provision of cooked meals to the remaining parts of the State. 
(b) Under the programme, Central Government provides food-grains, 
free of cost through Food Corporation of India and admissible transportation 
charges. Based on the Central Support, the conversion cost for converting 
the foodgrains into a meal is to be  borne by the concerned State/UT. For 
meeting the cost of foodgrains and transportation charges, an amount of 
Rs. 1175 crore has been provided in the budget for 2002-2003 by the 
Central Government. Cost of conversion etc. it to be met by the concerned 
State/UT. The Central Government has urged States/UTs which are 
currently providing dry rations to shift to providing a cooked meal. 
As per the available information, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry are providing cooked 
food. In Madhya Pradesh, meals are being served to children in 89 tribal 
blocks. In Orissa, meals are provided in 8 KBK districts (Bolangir, 
Kalahandi, Koraput, Malkangiri, Navrangpur, Nupada, Raigadaand Sonepur) 
and 74 ITDA blocks of non KBK districts. Karnataka is providing meals in 
Belari, Bidar, Bijapur, Bagalkote, Gulbarga, Kopala and Raichur districts 
while cooked meals are being provided  through an NGO called ISKCON to 
about 6000 children of Bangalore rural districts. Ready-to-eat food is being 
distributed in Delhi and Rajasthan. 
(c) As per the evaluation undertaken in 1999 in ten States by an 
independent agency called Operations Research Group, New Delhi, namely, 
Assam,Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West bengal, while the 
Mid-day Meal programme has given boost to enrolment in Assam, Madhya 
Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal and has had positive impact on 
attendance and retention on other six States. 
127

Besides, a study conducted by NCERT in year 2000 on State's policies 
on incentive schemes in primary schools and their contribution to girls' 
participation, also covered the Mid-day meal Scheme in Uttar Pradesh and 
Tamil Natdu. the report states that the noon-meal scheme of Tamil Nadu and 
supply of foodgrains under Mid-day Meal Scheme in Uttar Pradesh have 
helped improve the enrolment and retention of girls in schools.

368. SHRIAIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU):  
 DR. AKHILESH DAS:  
 DR. KARAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of students reported to have committed suicide, 
preceeding and following the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) 
and other equivalent examination resu lts this year, and the comparative 
figures for the preceding three years; 
(b) how far the examination system is considered responsible for heart-
break, depression and suicide of students; and 
(c) the steps taken so far and being taken to improve and reform the 
system? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) A 
few cases of suicides related to examin ation were reported in the newspapers 
after declaration of Board results this year. However, statistics in this regard are 
not reported to this Ministry. The cases relating to depression and suicides are 
linked to a number of factors including individual personality, fast changing 
social dynamics, home environment, inability of children to cope with the 
demands and expectations of family, peer pressure and a situation in which career 
opportunities are very limited in relation to mounting number of aspirants and 
examinations being a major determinant of career path. 
The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) has already taken several 
steps to help the students to overcome their difficulties like: 
* Arranging for a stress-free environment in schools 
* Deciding on introduction of life skill education 
* Elimanation of overall aggregation of marks to reduce unhealthy 
competition among students 
129 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
* Introduction of comprehensive and continuous school based 
evaluation 
* Providing facility of compartment examination in two subjects in 
Class X and one subject in Class XII 
* Providing three chances of compartment examination for Class X and 
XII 
* Restructuring of questions in some of the important subjects such as 
Science and Mathematics 
* Publication of sample question papers and marking schemes to 
familiarize teachers and students a bout the nature of questions and 
question papers. 
Similarly, the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examination 
(CISCE) has introduced measures like flexibility in the choice of subjects at the 
Secondary level, internal assess ment, continuous involvement of 
schools/teachers in updating and revising the prescribed curriculum etc. to 
facilitate learning and reducing stress on students. 
The CBSE has also started tele-couns elling on voluntary basis by the 
educationists, psychologists, psychiatrists and seasoned principals of the 
schools. It starts functioning before and during the examinations and also 
during declaration of results to mitigat e and defuse the sense of anxiety and 
stress among the students. For 2002 examinations, CBSE had started helpline 
from 31 centres in and outside the country. Recognising the importance of 
counselling parents in the matter, the CBSE has written to all CBSE affiliated 
schools for organizing such counselling sessions.

Statement-I 
Details of the Schemes for Women and Children being 
implemented by DWCD at present 
1 .  Scheme of Creches/Day tare Centres for children of working and ailing 
women 
It aims to provide day care services for the children (0—5 years) of mainly 
casual, migrant, agricultural and construction labourers. 
2. National Creche Fund 
It provides for a corpus fund to meet the growing requirement of 
opening more creche centres for working and ailing mothers. 
3. Hostels for working women 
Under the scheme financial assistance is given to voluntary 
Organisations, local bodies and cooperative institutions engaged in the field of 
women's/social welfare/women's educa tion. Public Sector Undertakings, 
Women Development Corporations, Educational Institutions and State 
Governments for the construction of hostels for working women in order to 
enable women seek employment and participate in technical training. 
4. Setting up ofemployment-cum-training-cum-lncome Generating Units 
for women (NORAD) 
Under this programme, financial assistance is given to Women's 
Development Corporations, Public Sector Corporations, autonomous bodies 
and voluntary organisations, to train poor women, mostly in non-traditional 
trades and to ensure their employment in this areas. 
5. Support to training and employment programme for women (STEP) 
This programme seeks to provide updated skills and new knoweldge to poor 
and assetless women in the traditional sectors, such as, agriculture animal 
husbandary, dairying, fisheries, handlooms, handicrafts, khadi and village 
industries, sericulture, social forestry and wasteland devleopment for enhancing, 
their productivity!and income generation. 
157 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 July, 2002] 
6. Short stay homes for women and girls 
The scheme seeks to protect and rehabilitate those women and girls 
who are facing social and moral danger due to family problems, mental 
strains, social ostracism, exploitation and other causes. 
7. Distance Education Programme 
The Scheme provides for a certifi cate course by IGNOU to train 
Women Self Help up workers. 
8. Condensed Courses of education and Vocational Training for women 
(CC&VT) 
The Scheme is implemented by the Central Social Welfare Board with 
the objective of providing basic education and skills to needy women and also to 
benefit widows destitute deserted women and also those belonging to 
economically backward classes. 
9. Awareness Generation Project (AGP) 
It aims to generate awareness among rural and poor women about their 
status in the family and society and to  activate them to work for achieving 
their rights and to deal with social issues. 
10. Scheme for women in difficult circumstances-Swadhar 
The schemes has been designed with a flexible and innovative approach 
to cater to the requirement of various types of women in distress in diverse 
situations under different conditions.

Injury proof coaches 
422. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Railways have developed coaches which are 
passenger-friendly and injury-proof in the event of accidents; 
(b) whether these coaches have been tried on passenger trains and have 
passed the desired tests; if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what are the special features which make these coaches injury proof 
and passenger-friendly; and 
(d) by when these coaches would be a ttached to all the important long-
distance Mail and Express trains? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Railway coaches of existing design 
have a number of amenity fittings for passenger comfort and have all steel 
welded bodies which are anti-telescopic to save passenger lives during 
accidents. However, to further improv e the crashworthin ess of coaches, 
railways have initiated a two pronged action. Firstly, a thorough review of 
coach interiors and fittings was carried out and innovative ideas were 
generated to modify the interiors so that no injury occurs during accidents. 
An inter-railway coach interiors modifications competition was held and 51 
such modifications were short listed for adoption on all coaches being 
manufactured or taken for periodic overhauling. Instructions have been issued 
to start implementation of such modifications short listed for adoption in new 
coaches as well as for retro-fitment on existing coaches. 
Also, a second action has been initiated to develop coaches with 
crashworthy bodies using computer simulation and field validation through 
actual crash tests. Once developed, such coaches will absorb a major part of 
impact during serious accidents in n on-passenger-carrying areas, thus saving 
precious human lives. 
(b) Some coaches with improved interiors have been inducted in 
service. The passenger reaction and impact of modification will be evaluated 
on continuing basis to improve further. As regards development of coaches 
with crashworthy bodies, such coaches will be evaluated 
202 

[19 July, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
through physical crash tests, conducted on prototype based on designs 
developed through computer simulation. 
(c) A list of 42 of modifications for improvement of interiors, to prevent 
injury to pasengers in case of accidents and another 9 modifications to prevent 
injury to passengers from climbing on coach roof is enclosed in the Statement. 
(See below) 
(d) These modifications to the interiors have already been adopted for new 
manufacture and also for retrofitment on existing coaches during every periodic 
overhaul. As the process of induction of improved coaches will be gradual and 
may need further improvements, no fixed time frame can be arranged for 
completion of this process at this stage, through all out efforts are made to 
carry out these changes early. 
The process of development of coaches with crashworthy structures is also 
in the preliminary stage and no target can be fixed at this stage for complete 
implementation on all important long distance Mail and Express trains.

consumption of stores and spares, improvement in other key techno-
economic parameters, etc. 
• Implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).

on customer satisfaction etc.

relating to statutory requirement like safety, environment etc.

Social Security for Dependent Aged 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Madam, India has a 
population of ten crore aged people, wh o are above sixty years. Out of them, 
40 per cent are living below the poverty line, and nearly 8 per cent of them are 
destitute. The physical and financial dependency of the aged is reported to be 
on the increase, as majority of them are not covered under any of the social 
security measures, like supplementary pe nsions, health insurance etc. It is 
estimated that 90 per cent of the aged in India are lacking social security 
measures. 
Medical care is the most import ant thing for which the aged need 
security measures. Vulnerabilities to diseases and disabilities increase as a 
person gets aged. It is reported that those who are aged between 65-74 years, 
suffer an average of 4.6 types of chronic conditions of which more than 60 per 
cent are multiple. For those above 75 year s, the mean number of ailments per 
person is 5.8. The cost of medical care  for a person with multiple disease 
problem ranges from Rs. 1500-10,000 a month, depending upon the severity 
of the problem. 
The National Old Age Pension Scheme, which is supposed to 
provide financial assistance to the elderly, has very limited coverage. The 
Government's target was to cover a population of 54,48,660 under this 
programme in the year 2001. But, the actual coverage in the year 2001 was 
only 2,06,810. Interventions through NGOs are also found to be very limited. 
Hence, the Government should come up with a comprehensive 
legislation, offering proper social security measures to the old , y more 
particularly, to the destitute old. Thank you.

Transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab 
SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nominated): Madam, my Special 
Mention pertains to non-transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab. As provided in 
clause 7 of the Rajiv-Longowal Accord, Chandigarh was to be transferred to 
Punjab and the transfer was to occur on 26 lh January, 1986.   It was 
stipulated that when Chandigarh goes to  Punjab, in lieu thereof some Hindi-
speaking areas in Punjab, which are cont iguous to Haryana, with village as a 
unit, would go to Haryana. Accordingly, a Commission was set up under 
Justice K.K. Mathew which was to give its verdict by 31 sl December, 1985. The 
Commission could not locate any such areas. Another Commission was 
appointed under Justice E.S. Venkataramiah on 2 nd April, 1986, to see if any 
Hindi-speaking villages contiguous to Haryana could be located. Justice 
Venkataramiah determined that 70,000 acres of land was due to Haryana 
against which he could earmark 45,000 acres comprising 30 Hindi-speaking 
villages contiguous to Haryana. As for the rest 25,000 acres, he 
recommended that Punjabi-speaking areas should be transferred to Haryana. 
It did not work. Another Commission unde r Justice D.A. Desai was appointed 
on 20m June, 1986, to determine the specific areas within 24 hours. He failed 
to do so. Since Punjab would not part with 25,000 acres of Punjabi-speaking 
area to Haryana, Chandigarh has remained untransferred and the Rajiv-
Longowal Accord unimplemented. 
My plea is that if Haryana must have its pound of flesh, 25,000 acres 
of land could be donated by Uttar Pradesh, a massive neighbour in the East, 
as a gesture of goodwill, and the dispute can be settled. I wonder why the 
Centre is not persuading Uttar Pradesh Government which is an ally of the 
NDA.

Lok. Sabha, in March, 2002, which has  now been referred to the Standing 
Parliamentary Committee on Human Resource Development. I propose that 
the official Bill be withdrawn and this Bill, which has the support of the 
women's organisations across the countr y be made the Government's Bill. In 
case this is too revolutionary a step a nd this can't be done, then I propose that 
this Bill of Smt. Sarla Maheshwari should also be sent to the Standing 
Committee on Human Resource Development to bear scrutiny so that they 
understand the significance  of the provisions that  Sarla Maheshwariji has 
spoken about, which must definitely be included in that Bill, if its purpose is not 
just to make a token measure towards women, but actually to redress the 
sufferings of victims of domestic violence. 
Smt. Rita Vermaji is also here and I would like to remind her that the 
hon. Minister, Shri Murli Manohar Joshi, on 8th  March, 2002, when Smt. 
Najma Heptullaji had spoken about the fact  that several women's groups were 
against this Bill-end I had spoken abqut it—in fact, assured us, "if there were 
certain misgivings that the women's grou ps have, we would be only too happy

There were certain points that had been discussed over there. 
Amongst them are certain non-negotiabl e points as compared with the 
Government's Bill which I find very necessary to specify here. Firstly, in the 
very definition of domestic violence, the comments that we made are that 
itshould be defined to mean any act, omission or conduct which is of such a

health, safety of the person which in cludes physical abuse, sexual abuse,

the various forms of domestic violence. This definition is based on the UN 
Model Code on Domestic Violence an d is representative of women's 
experiences of violence. It is univers ally accepted definition of domestic 
violence.  This is the first point. 
Secondly, in the Government's Bill t here is a plea of self-defence. All 
women groups are demanding the omission of clause 4(2) from the 
Government of India's Bill. It is absolutely non-negotiable and cannot be 
accepted. 
Then comes the right to reside in the shared household. What we 
are insisting on is that law must incl ude the right to reside in the shared 
household. Women will have a right not to be evicted or excluded from 
the household except in accordance with the law. If a woman is evicted, 
then she will have a right to enter t he household. She has a right to obtain 
protection order in the form of residence order. If she is being thrown out 
of the shared household or is being threatened of the same, then this is of 
vital importance because we have seen that many women continue to live in 
homes where they are the victims of  domestic violence only because they 
have no other place to go. The houses of their parents are closed for 
them. The State does not pr ovide any kind of shelter for them. There is no 
place to go. They continue to stay in that violent situation. If by law they 
can be given the right to reside in the same household till such time as law 
takes its course, it will become clearer and not something which, like Mr. 
Arun Jaitley argues, is there in the provisions in the j idgements of 
maintenance because you cannot rely on judgements.   You have to have a 
law that protects the right of women to reside within the same household. And 
we cannot rely on judgements. Mr. Ar un Jaitley argues t hat that right is 
included under maintenance. What happens  is that maintenance when it gets  
considered,   it   gets  translated   into  cash.     For  example,   if  the

prohibiting a respondent from aiding and abetting in the commission of such

Globally, violence within the home is universal cutting across culture, 
religion, class, and ethnicity. Despite this widespread prevalence, however, 
such violence is customarily acknowledged and has remained invisible - a 
problem thought unworthy of legal or political attention. According to the 
available statistics from around the gl obe, one out of every three women has 
experienced violence in an intimate relationship at some point in her life. The 
National Crimes Record Bureau, Minist ry of Home Affairs, Government of 
India reveals a shocking 71.5 per cent in crease in cases of torture during the

acquiesced and put up no resistance whatsoever.

cannot break up this marriage.'   So, this constant
